tips.title: Three kinds of impact, and say which is which
tips.body: **Ethical** is about right and wrong. **Legal** is about what the law permits. **Environmental** is about the physical world. A question naming one expects that one — label your points and you cannot drift.

tips.title: Give both sides, then judge
tips.body: These questions are marked for **balance**. Give a benefit, give a cost, then say which you think outweighs the other **and why**. A one-sided answer caps out low however well written.

tips.title: Ethical and legal are not the same
tips.body: Something can be **legal but unethical** — an app that legally collects far more data than it needs. Saying so explicitly is one of the easiest ways to show you understand the difference.

tips.title: Principles, not headlines
tips.body: The specification says you need the **general principles** behind the issues, **not detailed knowledge of specific issues**. So reason about *why* a technology creates a tension; do not try to memorise current news stories.

tips.title: The privacy argument has two real sides
tips.body: Citizens **value their privacy** and dislike too much government access. Governments argue they **cannot keep people safe** without it. The specification states **both**, so an answer giving only one has answered half the question.

steps.title: Three kinds of impact
steps.body:
**Digital technology changes society, and not only for the better.** The specification asks you to explain the **current ethical, legal and environmental impacts and risks** of digital technology, **including issues of privacy**.

**Ethical** — is it **right**? Questions about fairness, honesty, consent and harm. Ethics is about what people **ought** to do, whether or not anyone is forcing them.

**Legal** — is it **allowed**? What the law actually permits and forbids.

**Environmental** — what does it do to the **physical world**? Energy used, materials mined, equipment discarded.

**The crucial point is that ethical and legal are not the same thing.** A company may collect far more data about you than it needs, ask your consent in terms nobody reads, and be entirely within the law. That is **legal but arguably unethical**. Laws also lag behind technology, so new problems are often unregulated for years.

**Privacy** cuts across all three and is named separately in the specification. It is the question of **who knows what about you**, and whether you chose to let them.

**What the specification expects:** the **general principles behind the issues**, explicitly **not detailed knowledge of specific issues**. You are not required to know current news stories — you are required to reason.

Illegal and unethical
Ethical but illegal

check.solution: If the law permits it, it is **legal** — but collecting far more than is needed is hard to defend as **right**, so it is **legal but arguably unethical**. The two are separate tests.

steps.title: The eight areas
steps.body:
**Exam questions are taken from these eight areas**, and the specification lists them explicitly.

**Cyber security** — the cost of protecting systems, and the consequences when it fails. Who is responsible when data is lost?

**Mobile technologies** — always-connected devices. Convenience against constant **location tracking**, the expectation of being available at all hours, and the materials and energy behind replacing a phone every few years.

**Wireless networking** — convenient and mobile, but the signal **leaves the building**, so security depends on encryption rather than on physical access.

**Cloud storage** — files reachable anywhere, backed up by someone else. But the data sits on **another organisation's hardware**, possibly in **another country** under different laws, and the data centres consume very large amounts of **energy**.

**Hacking** — unauthorised access to a computer system. Clearly illegal; the interesting questions are about **degree** and **motive**, and about who bears the cost.

**Wearable technologies** — watches and fitness trackers collecting **continuous health data**. Useful to the wearer; valuable to insurers and employers, which is where the tension lies.

**Computer based implants** — devices inside the body, such as pacemakers. Life-changing benefits, and serious questions about **security** and **consent** when the device cannot simply be switched off.

**Autonomous vehicles** — potentially far safer than human drivers, but raising the question of **who is responsible** when one causes harm, and what happens to driving jobs.

steps.title: Privacy, and both sides of it
steps.body:
**The specification singles out privacy, and it gives both sides of the argument.**

> **Ordinary citizens** normally value their privacy and may not like governments or security services having too much access.

> **Governments and security services** often argue they cannot keep citizens safe from terrorism and other attacks without access to private data.

**Both positions are reasonable**, which is exactly why it is examined. This is not a case where one side is simply wrong.

**The citizens' case.** Privacy is not only for people with something to hide. Knowing you are watched changes how you behave — what you search for, what you say, what help you seek. Data gathered for one purpose tends to be used for others later. And any database that exists can be **leaked, stolen or misused** by a future government with different intentions.

**The security services' case.** Serious crimes are planned using the same encrypted, everyday technologies everyone uses. If those communications cannot be read even with a warrant, some attacks that could have been prevented will not be. The argument is not that privacy does not matter, but that it is **not the only thing that matters**.

**Why there is no clean answer.** Both positions value something real, and more of one generally means less of the other. Most practical proposals are about **where the line falls** and **who decides** — judicial oversight, warrants, time limits — rather than about abolishing either principle.

**In the exam**, give **both** sides. An answer presenting only one has answered half the question, however forcefully it argues.

steps.title: Structuring an answer
steps.body: **These questions are marked for balance and judgement.** The structure below works for any of the eight areas.

visuals.problem: Discuss the impacts of wearable fitness trackers on society.

steps.text: Say **which kind of impact** you are discussing, and label each point
steps.note: ethical, legal or environmental — a question naming one expects that one

steps.text: **Benefits:** the wearer sees their own activity and sleep, is encouraged to exercise, and a heart problem may be spotted early
steps.note: always start from the genuine benefit, or the answer reads as a complaint

steps.text: **Ethical costs:** the data is **continuous** and **medical**. An insurer could raise premiums using it; an employer could pressure staff to share it
steps.note: the tension is that the same data is useful to the wearer and valuable to others

steps.text: **Legal:** health data has extra protection in law, but consent is usually given through terms **nobody reads** — legal, and arguably not meaningful
steps.note: this is where legal and ethical come apart, so say so explicitly

steps.text: **Environmental:** materials mined for the device, energy to make and charge it, and **electronic waste** when it is replaced after two or three years
steps.note: the environmental point is often forgotten, and it is a whole mark

steps.text: **Judgement:** the benefits are real but fall to the **individual**, while the risks fall on those who never agreed — so the issue is control of the data, not the device
steps.note: name what your judgement rests on; that is what lifts a conclusion above "it depends"

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the three kinds of impact in the specification.
2. Give an example of something that is legal but arguably unethical.
3. State the two sides of the privacy argument.

**Part B.**

4. Give one ethical and one environmental impact of cloud storage.
5. Give one benefit and one risk of computer based implants.
6. Explain the main ethical difficulty with autonomous vehicles.

**Part C.**

7. Discuss the impacts of wearable technologies on society, reaching a judgement.
8. Explain why the law often struggles to keep up with new technology.
9. "Nothing to hide, nothing to fear." Evaluate this argument about privacy.

For question 9, consider whether privacy protects only wrongdoing.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Label each point.** Say *this is an ethical issue* or *this is an environmental impact*. Examiners mark against the kind of impact asked for, and labelling stops you drifting into a different one without noticing.

**Show that legal and ethical come apart.** An app that collects far more data than it needs, with consent buried in terms nobody reads, is **legal**. Whether it is **right** is a separate question, and stating that distinction explicitly is one of the quickest ways to show real understanding.

**Explain why the law lags.** Laws are written in response to problems that have already appeared, and take years to pass. Technology moves faster, so there is usually a period where something is **possible, harmful and not yet illegal**. That is a general principle, which is exactly what the specification asks for.

**Do not forget the environmental impact.** It is the one most often left out. Devices need **materials mined**, **energy to manufacture and run**, and become **electronic waste** when replaced. Data centres for cloud storage consume very large amounts of electricity. That is a whole strand of the question sitting unclaimed.

**Give both sides of privacy, fairly.** Citizens **value their privacy**; governments argue they **cannot keep people safe** without access. Presenting the other side weakly is a common way to lose the evaluation marks — the examiner is looking for whether you can state a view you disagree with accurately.

**Answer "nothing to hide, nothing to fear" properly.** Privacy protects far more than wrongdoing: medical conditions, relationships, what you searched for while frightened. Knowing you are observed **changes behaviour** even when you have done nothing wrong. And it assumes whoever holds the data will always be trustworthy and will never leak it — an assumption about the **future**, not the present.

**Ask who bears the cost.** The benefit of a wearable falls to the **wearer**; the risk may fall on people who never agreed. That question — **who gains and who pays** — turns a list into an argument.

**Reach a judgement and say what it rests on.** *On balance the benefits outweigh the risks, provided the data cannot be shared without explicit consent* is a conclusion. *There are arguments on both sides* is not.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Three kinds of impact: **ethical** (is it right), **legal** (is it allowed), **environmental** (what it costs the planet).
- **Privacy** is named separately and cuts across all three.
- **Legal and ethical are not the same** — something can be legal and still wrong.
- The law **lags behind** technology, so new harms are often unregulated at first.
- The eight areas: **cyber security**, **mobile technologies**, **wireless networking**, **cloud storage**, **hacking**, **wearable technologies**, **computer based implants**, **autonomous vehicles**.
- **Mobile technologies**: convenience against constant location tracking.
- **Cloud storage**: convenience against control, other countries' laws, and data centre **energy**.
- **Wearables**: useful to the wearer, valuable to **insurers and employers**.
- **Implants**: life-changing, but raise **security** and **consent** questions.
- **Autonomous vehicles**: safer overall, but **who is responsible** for harm?
- Environmental costs: **materials mined**, **energy used**, **electronic waste**.
- Privacy, side one: citizens **value privacy** and dislike too much government access.
- Privacy, side two: governments argue they **cannot keep citizens safe** without access.
- The specification wants **general principles**, not detailed knowledge of specific issues.
- Always **give both sides** and then reach a **justified judgement**.

questions.prompt: Discuss the ethical, legal and environmental impacts of cloud storage on individuals and organisations.
questions.solution:
Cloud storage keeps files on **magnetic and/or solid state storage at a remote location**, reached over a network. Its benefits are real: files are available from **any device anywhere**, they are **easy to share**, the provider handles **backups** and failed hardware, and capacity can be expanded without buying anything.

**Ethically**, the central issue is **control**. The data is held on **another organisation's hardware**, so the owner is trusting that company's security, its staff, and its continued existence. If the provider is breached, the loss falls on people who never chose that provider — a school's pupils, or a company's customers.

A second ethical concern is what the provider does with the data. Many services are free because the data has value, and the **consent** for that is usually given through terms almost nobody reads. That consent may be legally valid while not being a meaningful choice, and an organisation putting **other people's** data into such a service is making that decision on their behalf.

**Legally**, the servers may be in **another country**, under different data protection laws, where local authorities may have rights of access that would not exist at home. Responsibility is also less clear than it appears: if the provider is breached, the organisation that chose to use them generally remains **responsible to the people whose data was lost**, even though it did not run the system that failed. Laws on data protection exist and are enforced, but they were largely written for data held on your own premises, and the **law lags** behind arrangements like this.

**Environmentally**, cloud storage means **data centres**, which consume very large amounts of **electricity** — both to run the servers and to **cool** them. Servers are replaced on a cycle of a few years, so there is also continual **electronic waste** and continual demand for the **materials** used to build them.

The honest comparison, though, is not against nothing: it is against every organisation running its own servers instead. Large data centres are generally **more efficient** per unit of storage than many small server rooms, and they are increasingly sited to use renewable power. So the environmental effect of cloud storage specifically may be **better** than the alternative, even though the absolute figures are alarming.

**Judgement.** For most individuals and small organisations, the benefits of cloud storage outweigh the costs, and the environmental argument is probably in its favour rather than against. But that holds **only where the data is not especially sensitive**. For confidential records — medical, financial, or data about children — the loss of **control** and the **jurisdiction** question weigh much more heavily, and the decision should turn on whether the people the data is about would consider it reasonable, not merely on whether it is legal and convenient.

questions.prompt: Discuss the argument that security services should have access to private communications, considering the views of both citizens and governments.
questions.solution:
This is a genuine disagreement in which **both sides value something real**, which is why it is worth examining rather than simply settling.

**The citizens' position.** The specification notes that ordinary citizens **normally value their privacy and may not like it when governments or security services have too much access**. The strongest version of this argument is not about hiding wrongdoing. Privacy protects **medical conditions, relationships, beliefs, and the searches people make when frightened or ashamed** — none of which is criminal, and all of which people reasonably keep to themselves.

Being observed also **changes behaviour**. People look things up less freely, and seek help less readily, if they believe a record is being kept. That cost falls on the innocent, and falls hardest on those who most need help.

There are two further arguments. Data gathered for one stated purpose has a tendency to be **used for others later**, without anyone re-consulting those it concerns. And any database that exists can be **leaked, stolen, or inherited by a future government with different intentions** — so the question is not only whether today's authorities are trustworthy, but whether every future holder of that data will be.

**The governments' position.** The specification is equally clear that governments and security services **often argue that they cannot keep their citizens safe from terrorism and other attacks unless they have access to private data**. Serious crimes are now planned using the same encrypted, ordinary services everyone uses. If those communications cannot be read even with a **warrant**, then some attacks that could have been prevented will not be, and the cost of that also falls on innocent people.

It is worth stating this side fairly: the claim is not that privacy is unimportant, but that it is **not the only thing that matters**, and that safety is also a condition of a free life. Most governments also accept that access should be **subject to safeguards** rather than unlimited.

**Evaluation.** The difficulty is that the two values **trade off**: more access means less privacy, and more privacy means less access. Neither can be maximised without cost to the other, so any position is a judgement about **where the line falls**.

Two observations help. First, the technical argument is often overstated on the government side — a system built so that authorities can read encrypted messages is, by construction, a system with a deliberate weakness in it, and that weakness is available to **attackers and hostile states** as well. There is no way to weaken encryption only for the people you trust.

Second, the citizens' argument is strongest about **bulk** collection and weakest about **targeted** access. Reading one named suspect's messages under a judge's warrant is a different proposition from retaining everyone's communications by default.

**Conclusion.** On balance I would allow **targeted** access, authorised in advance by a court, time-limited, and subject to independent oversight — but not **general** access to everyone's communications, and not a mandated weakness in encryption itself. That position takes the security argument seriously where it is strongest, while refusing the measures whose costs fall almost entirely on people who have done nothing wrong. What it rests on is the distinction between **suspicion** and **surveillance**: the state should be able to investigate a person it has reason to suspect, without treating the whole population as suspects in advance.

Being observed also **changes behaviour**. People look things up less freely, and seek help less readily, if they believe a record is being kept. That cost falls on the innocent, and falls hardest on those who most need help.

There are two further arguments. Data gathered for one stated purpose has a tendency to be **used for others later**, without anyone re-consulting those it concerns. And any database that exists can be **leaked, stolen, or inherited by a future government with different intentions** — so the question is not only whether today's authorities are trustworthy, but whether every future holder of that data will be.

**The governments' position.** The specification is equally clear that governments and security services **often argue that they cannot keep their citizens safe from terrorism and other attacks unless they have access to private data**. Serious crimes are now planned using the same encrypted, ordinary services everyone uses. If those communications cannot be read even with a **warrant**, then some attacks that could have been prevented will not be, and the cost of that also falls on innocent people.

It is worth stating this side fairly: the claim is not that privacy is unimportant, but that it is **not the only thing that matters**, and that safety is also a condition of a free life. Most governments also accept that access should be **subject to safeguards** rather than unlimited.

**Evaluation.** The difficulty is that the two values **trade off**: more access means less privacy, and more privacy means less access. Neither can be maximised without cost to the other, so any position is a judgement about **where the line falls**.

Two observations help. First, the technical argument is often overstated on the government side — a system built so that authorities can read encrypted messages is, by construction, a system with a deliberate weakness in it, and that weakness is available to **attackers and hostile states** as well. There is no way to weaken encryption only for the people you trust.

Second, the citizens' argument is strongest about **bulk** collection and weakest about **targeted** access. Reading one named suspect's messages under a judge's warrant is a different proposition from retaining everyone's communications by default.

**Conclusion.** On balance I would allow **targeted** access, authorised in advance by a court, time-limited, and subject to independent oversight — but not **general** access to everyone's communications, and not a mandated weakness in encryption itself. That position takes the security argument seriously where it is strongest, while refusing the measures whose costs fall almost entirely on people who have done nothing wrong. What it rests on is the distinction between **suspicion** and **surveillance**: the state should be able to investigate a person it has reason to suspect, without treating the whole population as suspects in advance.

examTechnique.body:
**Label each point** as ethical, legal or environmental. Give **both sides**, then reach a **judgement and say what it rests on** — a list without a conclusion cannot reach the top band.

Remember the **environmental** strand, which is the one most often dropped, and show that **legal and ethical are not the same**.
examinerErrors: Mixing the three kinds of impact without labelling them.
Treating legal and ethical as one and the same.
Leaving out the environmental impact entirely.
Giving only one side of the privacy argument.
Reciting news stories instead of reasoning from principles.
Accepting "nothing to hide, nothing to fear" without examining it.
Ending with "there are arguments on both sides" and no judgement.
Presenting the opposing view weakly so it can be dismissed.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer **labels** each point as ethical, legal or environmental, and shows it understands the distinction by naming something **legal but arguably unethical** — consent buried in unread terms. It never drops the **environmental** strand: materials, energy, electronic waste. On privacy it states **both** sides **fairly**, including the one it goes on to reject, and it tests slogans rather than repeating them, noting that privacy protects far more than wrongdoing and that any database can be leaked or inherited. It asks **who gains and who pays**, and it ends with a **judgement** that names what it rests on, rather than observing that there are two sides.
